title: Managing illness in practice
goal: Apply the neck check, plan a return after illness, and name the habits (hygiene, sleep, energy, carbohydrate) that lower illness risk in athletes.

steps.title: The neck check
steps.text:
The [neck check](g:neck-check) is a rule many sports doctors use [[c:neck-rule]]. Symptoms only above the neck (runny nose, sneezing, mild sore throat)? An easy session is usually fine. Symptoms below the neck (fever, chest tightness, deep cough, aching body)? The usual advice is rest. Chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath or a racing, skipping heartbeat: stop and see a doctor [[c:cardiac-stop]].

The worry is [myocarditis](g:myocarditis), a virus-inflamed heart muscle. It is the main serious risk of hard exercise during a viral illness [[c:myo-main]], but rare: one death from it per 2.3 million person-years of sport [[c:myo-rare]]. Be clear about the evidence: the neck check was never tested, and return-to-sport rules rest on expert opinion [[c:expert-opinion]].

claims.text: The neck-check rule is commonly used by sports physicians: exercise is allowed if symptoms are limited to the upper respiratory tract.

evidence.quote: exercise is allowed if symptoms are limited to the upper respiratory tract

claims.text: Chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath and palpitations are absolute contraindications to exercise and a reason for heart tests.

evidence.quote: symptoms of cardiac involvement i.e., chest pain, syncope, shortness of breath, and palpitations are absolute contraindications for exercise and indications for cardiologic investigations

claims.text: Myocarditis is the main potentially severe health risk for athletes with a viral respiratory illness.

evidence.quote: Myocarditis is the main potentially severe health risk in athletes with a viral ARI.

claims.text: A systematic review found 1 sports-related death from myocarditis in 2.3 million person-years.

evidence.quote: The incidence was 0.047 per 100,000 person-years or 1 death of myocarditis in 2.3 million person-years.

claims.text: Guidelines for return to sport after a viral respiratory illness are based on expert opinion.

evidence.quote: Guidelines to return to sport after a viral ARI are based on expert opinions.
This rule is nonscientific but may be partly useful.

steps.title: Coming back after illness
steps.text:
No trial says how many days to wait. The plan below is common practice, not a tested protocol:

1. Wait until the illness symptoms are gone.
2. Start with short, easy sessions.
3. Add volume first, then intensity, in steps over days.
4. If symptoms return, drop back one step.

This is the same staged idea as the return to running after an injury. General guidance for load also says to raise volume gradually [[c:gradual]]. With flu, COVID-19 or a severe sore throat, see a doctor: return should rest on finding the cause, and some of these viruses can affect the heart [[c:diagnosis]].

claims.text: Consensus guidance for training and immune health: raise training volume and load gradually.

evidence.quote: employ a gradual and periodised increase in training volumes and loads

claims.text: Return to play after a viral respiratory illness should be based on diagnosing the cause; flu, COVID-19 and some other viruses can affect the heart and call for a break.

evidence.quote: Return to play should be based on etiologic diagnostics.
Potentially cardiogenic SARS-CoV-2, adenovirus, enterovirus, or influenza virus infections are reasons for a break in training and restriction of competitions.

steps.title: Hygiene and exposure
steps.text:
Athletes meet more germs than most people [[c:exposure]]: travel, shared housing, stuffy indoor rooms, shared meals, contact sports and mass events. Respiratory viruses spread by close contact through the air and on surfaces [[c:spread]].

So wash your hands often, especially after travel and before food. Do not share bottles or towels. Keep your distance from sick people, air indoor rooms, and stay away from team sessions when you are ill. At Tokyo 2020, comprehensive countermeasures helped limit COVID-19 [[c:tokyo-counter]], but that was one uncontrolled report.

claims.text: Athletes are more exposed to respiratory viruses than the general population.

evidence.quote: Athletes are more exposed than the general population because of increased verbal interaction and close physical contact during travel, shared housing, indoor spaces with poor ventilation, meal sharing in restaurants, high-contact-risk sports, and mass gatherings.

claims.text: Respiratory virus infections spread mostly by close contact, through the air and on surfaces.

evidence.quote: Respiratory virus infections are mostly spread by means of close physical contact through the air and on surfaces

claims.text: At Tokyo 2020, comprehensive countermeasures helped mitigate COVID-19 and exertional heat illness.

evidence.quote: Comprehensive countermeasures helped mitigate both COVID-19 and exertional heat illnesses.

steps.title: Sleep, stress, energy and the calendar

claims.text: Heavy exercise and life stress influence immune function through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the sympathetic nervous system.

evidence.quote: Challenges athletes face such as heavy exercise and life stress influence immune function via activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the sympathetic nervous system and the resulting immunoregulatory hormones.

claims.text: Sleep is an important part of recovery, but more research is needed on how sleep disruption affects athletes' immune systems.

evidence.quote: Sleep is an important aspect of recovery, but more research is needed to determine how sleep disruption influences the immune system of athletes.

claims.text: Athletes should be alert to periods of higher illness risk: intensive training weeks, the taper before competition, and competition itself.

evidence.quote: Athletes, coaches and medical personnel should be alert to periods of increased risk of illness (e.g. intensive training weeks, the taper period prior to competition, and during competition)

steps.title: Carbohydrate and food first
steps.text:
Carbohydrate during long, hard sessions is the best-supported nutrition tool for immunity [[c:carb-immune]]. It softens the stress-hormone rise and the swing in blood immune cells. Those are markers: whether they mean fewer colds is not yet shown [[c:carb-unproven]]. The fueling lessons give amounts.

Beyond that, food comes first: enough energy, protein and variety. Supplements are for a confirmed deficiency, such as low [vitamin D](g:vitamin-d) or iron [[c:food-first]]. Vitamin D is covered in the supplements lessons, so it is not repeated here.

claims.text: Carbohydrate supplementation is the most effective nutritional strategy for minimising immune disturbances during recovery from exercise.

evidence.quote: carbohydrate supplementation is the most effective for minimizing immune disturbances during exercise recovery
carbohydrate compared to placebo ingestion is associated with higher plasma glucose levels, an attenuated cortisol and growth hormone response, fewer perturbations in blood immune cell counts

claims.text: Whether the smaller immune changes with carbohydrate mean less illness awaits further research.

evidence.quote: although clinical significance awaits further research

claims.text: Quality nutrition is preferred over supplements, which are limited to identified deficiencies such as vitamin D or iron.

evidence.quote: Quality nutrition is preferred over the use of dietary supplements, which are limited to cases of identified deficiencies (e.g. vitamin D or iron deficiencies).

points: Neck check: symptoms only above the neck allow an easy session; fever, chest or body symptoms mean rest. It is expert opinion, not trial-based.
After illness, restart with short easy sessions and add volume, then intensity, in steps; a serious illness needs the doctor's advice.
Athletes are exposed to many germs: wash hands, do not share bottles, keep away from sick people, and stay home when ill.
Sleep, enough energy, life stress and the weeks of intensive training, taper and competition drive risk.
Carbohydrate during long sessions softens the immune swing; otherwise food first, supplements only for a confirmed deficiency.

variants.stem: A runner has a runny nose and sneezing, no fever, and normal energy. Under the neck check, what is reasonable?

options.text: An easy 30 min run, stopping if symptoms worsen
options.why: Right: symptoms are only above the neck.

options.text: A hard interval session to sweat it out
options.why: Hard exercise is not advised even with mild symptoms; the rule allows easy sessions.

options.text: Complete rest for at least a week
options.why: The rule allows light exercise when symptoms stay above the neck.

options.text: A race, since mild symptoms never matter
options.why: Racing is a hard effort; the rule covers easy sessions only.

variants.stem: A triathlete has a fever of 38.2 °C, aching legs and a chest cough. Under the neck check, what is the right call?

options.text: An easy swim, since swimming is gentle
options.why: Fever and chest symptoms mean rest, whatever the sport.

options.text: Rest and see a doctor if it does not settle
options.why: Right: symptoms below the neck mean no training.

options.text: A hard brick session to clear the chest
options.why: Hard exercise with fever is the case the rule exists to prevent.

options.text: A run, since cough alone never matters
options.why: Chest symptoms are a stop sign under the rule.

variants.stem: How strong is the evidence behind the neck check?

options.text: Weak: expert opinion, not trials
options.why: Right: the review calls the rule nonscientific and says return-to-sport guidelines rest on expert opinion.

options.text: Strong: several randomised trials
options.why: No such trials were found in the review.

options.text: Strong: myocarditis registries proved it
options.why: Registries show myocarditis is rare; they did not test the rule.

options.text: Proven: the IOC statement is built on it
options.why: The IOC load statement is about load, not this rule.

variants.stem: Why do doctors worry about hard exercise during a viral illness?

options.text: It makes the virus spread to the leg muscles
options.why: Exercise does not carry the virus to the legs.

options.text: Rare myocarditis: the virus may inflame the heart muscle
options.why: Right: myocarditis is the main serious risk, and it is rare.

options.text: It uses up all the antibodies you have
options.why: Antibodies are not used up by exercise.

options.text: It turns a cold into pneumonia in most athletes
options.why: Most colds do not become pneumonia, and that is not the concern here.

variants.stem: A cyclist had a cold for four days and is symptom-free today. What is the best plan for the first week back?

options.text: Short easy rides first, then volume, then intensity, in steps
options.why: Right: staged return, symptoms as the guide.

options.text: Squeeze in all the missed sessions in two days
options.why: Cramming raises stress when the body is least ready.

options.text: Wait for a blood test to show normal lymphocytes
options.why: Blood counts are not used to decide, and they swing with exercise anyway.

options.text: Go back to full intensity on day one to prove fitness
options.why: Jumping straight to full load is the opposite of a staged return.

variants.stem: Which habit best cuts the spread of colds in a team on a training camp?

options.text: Washing hands, not sharing bottles, and staying away when ill
options.why: Right: it targets contact and surface spread.

options.text: Doing extra hard sessions to toughen up the immune system
options.why: Extra load adds stress and does not block spread.

options.text: Taking cold showers after every session
options.why: There is no evidence this stops germs spreading.

options.text: Sharing one large bottle so all drink the same mix
options.why: Sharing bottles passes germs on.

variants.stem: Why might an athlete catch more colds than a desk worker, even with a healthy immune system?

options.text: Athletes have faulty immune cells
options.why: Nothing shows athletes' immune systems are faulty.

options.text: Athletes have less mucus in the nose
options.why: This is not an established cause of colds.

options.text: More exposure: travel, shared housing and crowds
options.why: Right: exposure is higher for athletes.

options.text: Sweating washes away the body's defences
options.why: Sweat does not remove immune defences.

variants.stem: In a winter block a rider sleeps 5.5 h, has a work deadline, and is cutting food to lose weight. What first step best lowers illness risk?

options.text: Protect sleep and eat enough before adding any supplement
options.why: Right: low energy and stress are listed risk factors and sleep aids recovery; a supplement cannot replace them.

options.text: Add a high-dose immune supplement
options.why: Supplements do not make up for poor sleep and low energy.

options.text: Train harder to toughen up
options.why: More load adds to the stress.

options.text: Stop all training for the whole block
options.why: Moderate training is protective; the aim is to fix the stressors.

variants.stem: Which periods does the consensus statement flag as higher risk for illness?

options.text: Easy recovery weeks and rest days only
options.why: Recovery weeks lower the stress, not raise the risk.

options.text: The off-season break after the last race
options.why: The flagged periods are during training and competing.

options.text: Intensive training weeks, the taper and competition
options.why: Right: these are the three listed periods.

options.text: The first week of a new base training block
options.why: This is not one of the periods named.

variants.stem: A brand says its carbohydrate drink prevents colds. What best fits the evidence?

options.text: It softens the immune swing in long sessions; fewer colds is not shown
options.why: Right: the effect is on markers; the clinical link awaits research.

options.text: Correct: carbohydrate prevents colds in all athletes
options.why: This goes beyond the evidence, which concerns markers.

options.text: Wrong: carbohydrate has no effect on immune markers
options.why: It does lower the stress-hormone and cell-count changes.

options.text: Correct, but only if taken with vitamin C
options.why: This is not supported by the sources used here.

variants.stem: A triathlete takes six immune supplements 'just in case', but blood tests show normal vitamin D and iron. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Focus on food and sleep; keep supplements for confirmed deficiencies
options.why: Right: food first, supplements only when a deficiency is identified.

options.text: Add more supplements, since more is safer
options.why: There is no evidence that more helps without a deficiency.

options.text: Swap them for one high-dose immune supplement
options.why: Without a deficiency, a bigger dose of one supplement has not been shown to help.

options.text: Take the supplements only on race days
options.why: Timing does not fix the lack of a deficiency.
